h1:
Sisaket Local Sweets
Sao-Ang, Durian Treats, and Market Street Snacks
intro: Sisaket isn't only about savory food — its sweets have a story of their own. As a four-ethnic-group province (Lao, Suay, Khmer, and Yoe), many of its desserts have roots in Khmer and truly local culture and are hard to find anywhere else. Add the volcanic durian season, which turns processed durian treats into a signature local souvenir, and you have plenty to try. We walked the markets and tracked down the shops so we can tell you which local sweets are worth a bite, where to buy processed durian, and what market street snacks are worth grabbing on the go.

blocks.html: Sisaket's sweets break down roughly into three groups. The first is the local Khmer- and four-ethnic-rooted sweets that are genuinely unique to the province, like sao-ang (also called khanom pad). The second is processed treats made from volcanic durian, which you can buy almost year-round even out of season. The last is the standard desserts and street snacks at the evening markets and walking street that are cheap and easy to grab. We'll go through each group in turn and tell you straight which ones are hard to find, which are easy to buy, and which shops are actually open right now.

blocks.text: Local sweets worth trying at least once

blocks.html: If you've come all the way to Sisaket, the local sweets are something you shouldn't walk past — many of them exist only here and are getting harder to find every year. We've picked them out one by one, ordered from the most famous and most worth trying first, down to the old-fashioned ones that are more of a curiosity.

items.name: Sao-ang (khanom pad)
items.blurb: Sisaket's legendary sweet, with Khmer cultural roots. It's a stirred flour paste grilled until fragrant — chewy, with just the right balance of sweet and rich. It was once voted Sisaket's signature local dish in the 'one province, one dish' campaign. If you only try one local sweet here, make it this one.

items.name: Dok lamduan cookies
items.blurb: Cookies shaped like the dok lamduan, the flower that symbolizes Sisaket. Crisp yet soft, lightly sweet, with the scent of jasmine-candle smoke. They work both as a snack and as a good-looking souvenir worth carrying home.

items.name: Khanom nang let (khao taen)
items.blurb: Pressed sticky-rice discs fried crisp and drizzled with cane syrup — sweet, crunchy, and moreish. A well-known local product and a souvenir that keeps for a long time. Good to snack on along the way too.

items.name: Khanom tot ma
items.blurb: An old-fashioned sweet with an odd name (literally 'dog fart') that many younger people have never tried. Made from local fruit steamed or grilled until fragrant, with a homely sweet-rich flavor. It's hard to find, so if you spot it, give it a taste.

blocks.title: Some local sweets are seasonal
blocks.html: Sweets like sao-ang and tot ma aren't sold every day at every shop. Sometimes you'll only find them at the Saturday walking street, cultural events, or specific makers. If you're really set on trying them, call the shop or check their page before you set off so you don't make the trip for nothing.

blocks.title: Want to taste deeper? Try a Sisaket food tour or cooking class
blocks.text: Half a day with a local who knows the lanes — or cooking a dish yourself — teaches you more than just eating. Book ahead on Klook or GetYourGuide.

blocks.text: Local sweet shops and souvenir spots that are actually open

blocks.html: Local sweets taste best and are most reliable when you buy from shops that make them seriously. We've gone through the places that are still open and that locals actually go to — some in-town spots that are easy to drop by, and some original-recipe makers a bit further out but more authentic. We've ordered them by how convenient they are to reach.

items.name: Mae Si Mart (Sao-Ang 4 Ethnic Groups)
items.blurb: The easiest sao-ang shop to find in town, near the Mae Si Sa Phom roundabout in Mueang Nuea subdistrict, Mueang district. They sell khanom pad by the piece and by the box, with several fillings and flavors per box so you can try them all in one go. Good to sample first, then buy a box as a souvenir. They also sell woven crafts and four-ethnic-group souvenirs, so one stop covers a lot.
items.meta: Mae Si Sa Phom roundabout, Mueang Nuea subdistrict, Mueang district · call to check before going 082-094-3919

items.name: Baan Khanom Rakhang Thong
items.blurb: A well-known Sisaket souvenir shop on Wichit Nakhon Road in town, famous for its own-recipe dok lamduan cookies — lightly sweet, crisp yet soft. They also have fresh mooncake-style pastries, pan sip, silkworm-cocoon cookies, shallot cookies, and during durian season, mooncakes filled with volcanic durian. A good place to stock up on a full range of souvenirs in one shop.
items.meta: Wichit Nakhon Rd, Mueang district · open most days during the daytime

items.name: Kwae Village — original sao-ang
items.blurb: An original-recipe sao-ang maker over in Khukhan district that makes homemade khanom pad and takes preserving the four-ethnic-group sweets seriously. If you want the real original and don't mind the distance, this is the source. But if you're in town and don't want to drive far, Mae Si Mart in town has a very similar taste.
items.meta: Khukhan district (a fair way from the city) · check the shop's page before going
items.price: Khanom pad by piece/box, prices similar to in town

items.name: Sri Fah Bakery
items.blurb: A long-running bakery in town that Sisaket locals know well, with fresh bread, cakes, and baked goods at friendly prices. Good for anyone wanting bakery-style sweets during the day, or grabbing bread for breakfast before heading out.

items.name: Waan Phodee (Thai dessert cafe)
items.blurb: A Thai-dessert cafe in the center of town with a relaxed sit-down feel, serving freshly made Thai sweets — bua loi, coconut-milk desserts, and cold options. Good for a break from the heat in the afternoon, or to finish a meal with a proper seat rather than just eating on the go.
items.meta: Central Sisaket town · open late morning to evening

items.name: Old markets & community markets (seasonal local sweets)
items.blurb: Beyond the regular shops, the community and old markets around the province often have vendors making local sweets on a seasonal basis — khanom sai sai, sticky-rice parcels, khanom tan, and hard-to-find festival sweets. Cheap, and genuinely handmade. Ask your accommodation which neighborhood has a community market on at the time.
items.meta: Rotates by day/by area · ask your accommodation

blocks.text: Volcanic durian treats — the province's signature sweet

blocks.html: Sisaket's volcanic durian is grown around Kantharalak, Khun Han, and Si Rattana, on soil weathered from old volcanic rock — the flesh is dry, fine-textured, sweet and rich with a milder smell. When durian season arrives (roughly May to July), fruit that's off-grade or floods the market gets processed, so there are durian treats on sale almost year-round even out of season. Anyone who misses the fresh-durian season can still get a taste in processed form.

items: Durian paste — durian flesh stirred down thick, sweet and rich, pressed into sheets or blocks. Keeps for a long time and is a popular souvenir you can carry on a plane or send by post.
Fried/crisp durian — durian sliced thin and fried or baked crisp, easy to snack on, with a milder smell than fresh durian. People who aren't brave enough for the fresh stuff can usually handle this.
Durian ice cream — ice cream made with real durian, found at the durian orchards that double as cafes and at some souvenir shops. Good for cooling off in durian season.
Durian-filled mooncakes — fresh mooncake pastries filled with volcanic durian, found at in-town souvenir shops during durian season, like Baan Khanom Rakhang Thong.
Frozen durian — for those who want fresh flesh but come out of season, some orchards and shops sell it frozen in packs; once thawed, the texture is still close to fresh.

blocks.title: Where to buy processed durian reliably
blocks.html: If you're passing through Kantharalak or Khun Han during durian season, just drop by an orchard that runs as a cafe, like Baan Suan Win Kawa — you can eat it fresh and buy processed durian straight from the orchard. In town, look for souvenir shops with the volcanic durian GI certification mark so you get the real thing from the actual source. Fresh durian prices rise and fall with the year and ripeness, so always ask the per-kilo price first.

If you don't feel like hunting down rare sweets, just walking the evening market or the walking street gives you plenty of desserts and snacks to grab — a few baht a bag, perfect to eat on the go or to round off dinner. These are the ones you'll see often and that locals actually buy.

items: Khanom krok, khanom thuai, khanom bueang — cart desserts made fresh and hot right in front of you, fragrant with coconut milk, easy to eat on the go. An easy way to finish off dinner.
Bua loi, lod chong, ruam mit in coconut milk — cold desserts to beat the heat; there's warm ginger-broth bua loi too, so pick to suit the weather.

Grilled banana, grilled sticky rice, khao jee — homely grilled sweets — grilled sticky rice with banana or taro filling, and khao jee brushed with egg and grilled fragrant — a snack for wandering the market.
Fried banana, fried taro, fried sweet potato, fried khao mao — sweet fritters in crisp batter, fried fresh, a few baht a bag, easy to grab and eat as you walk.
Roti, smoothies, seasonal fruit juice — banana-egg roti drizzled with condensed milk, cold smoothies, and seasonal fruit juice at the evening market — popular heat-beating sweets.

blocks.title: Carry cash and small notes
blocks.html: Most cart dessert vendors and market sellers still mainly take cash. Some have PromptPay but not all do, so coins and small notes will be handier — especially for snacks that cost five to twenty baht a bag.

If you want to try the local sweets and processed durian thoroughly without wearing yourself out, here's a two-day plan organized by zone. Day one covers the town, day two heads out to the durian-orchard side. Adjust the timing to the day you arrive — if it falls on a Saturday, keep the first evening free for the walking street.

items.activity: Start at Sri Fah Bakery or a morning sweet shop
items.note: Grab bread or baked goods to line your stomach before a full day of dessert hunting

items.activity: Drop by Mae Si Mart to try sao-ang
items.note: Buy khanom pad by the box so you can try several fillings, and snap photos of the four-ethnic-group crafts while you're there

items.activity: Hit Baan Khanom Rakhang Thong to stock up on souvenirs
items.note: Dok lamduan cookies, mooncake pastries, and durian-filled mooncakes during durian season

items.activity: Take a break at Waan Phodee
items.note: Order cold Thai desserts to beat the afternoon heat before heading to the evening market

items.activity: Walk the evening market or walking street (if it's Saturday)
items.note: Grab snacks — khanom krok, bua loi, grilled banana — and look out for local sweets you won't find on weekdays

items.activity: Drive out to the Kantharalak–Khun Han side
items.note: It's a fair drive from town, so fill up on fuel and check the route before you set off

items.activity: Stop at a durian orchard that runs as a cafe, like Baan Suan Win Kawa
items.note: In durian season you can eat it fresh from the orchard; out of season there's still processed durian and durian ice cream
Durian paste, fried durian, or frozen — pick whatever's easiest to carry home, and ask how to store it before buying

items.activity: Stop at a community market or souvenir shop on the way back
items.note: Pick up local sweets you haven't tried yet, like khanom nang let or the community's seasonal sweets

blocks.text: Tasting Sisaket sweets like a local, the smart way

items: For hard-to-find local sweets like sao-ang and tot ma, call the shop or check their page first, since some are made to order or only available seasonally.
Fresh durian is only around in durian season, roughly May to July. If you come out of season, focus on the processed treats instead — you'll still get that volcanic durian flavor.
Look for the volcanic durian GI certification mark when buying durian souvenirs, so you get the real thing from the actual source and not durian from elsewhere.
With market desserts, buy a little of many things so you get to try a variety without filling up too soon.
Fresh sweet souvenirs like mooncake pastries have a short shelf life — ask the expiry date and how to store them before carrying them far. Durian paste and khanom nang let keep longer.

blocks.title: If you're heading on toward the border
blocks.html: Plenty of people hunt sweets in town and then drive south the next day to Pha Mo I Daeng or Khao Phra Wihan National Park. We'll be straight with you: that border area has stretches that are sometimes closed or restricted. Always check the situation and whether the area is open before you travel, and have a backup plan ready.

faq.q: What local Sisaket sweets should I try?
faq.a: The most famous is sao-ang (khanom pad), a Khmer-rooted local sweet that's a stirred flour paste grilled until fragrant — it was once voted the province's signature local dish. Next are dok lamduan cookies shaped like the city's symbolic flower, khanom nang let (khao taen), and khanom tot ma, an old-fashioned sweet with an odd name. Many are seasonal, so ask the shop or check the Saturday walking street.

faq.q: Where can I buy sao-ang in Sisaket?
faq.a: In town, drop by Mae Si Mart near the Mae Si Sa Phom roundabout in Mueang Nuea subdistrict, Mueang district, which sells khanom pad by the piece and by the box with several fillings. The original maker is over in Khukhan district at Kwae Village. This kind of local sweet is sometimes made to order, so it's worth calling ahead before you go.

faq.q: Can I still eat durian in Sisaket outside durian season?
faq.a: Yes. Although fresh durian is only around roughly May to July, processed treats made from volcanic durian are on sale almost year-round — durian paste, crisp fried durian, durian ice cream, durian-filled mooncakes, and frozen durian — found at in-town souvenir shops and at durian orchards that double as cafes.

faq.q: Where can I find the most complete range of Sisaket sweet souvenirs?
faq.a: Baan Khanom Rakhang Thong on Wichit Nakhon Road in town is the shop with the fullest range — own-recipe dok lamduan cookies, mooncake pastries, pan sip, shallot cookies, and during durian season, volcanic durian-filled mooncakes. For sao-ang, you'll need to head separately to Mae Si Mart.

faq.q: What desserts are there at Sisaket's evening markets?
faq.a: All the standard cart desserts — khanom krok, khanom thuai, bua loi, lod chong, grilled banana, grilled sticky rice, sweet fritters like fried banana and fried sweet potato, and seasonal fruit juices and smoothies. A few baht a bag, perfect to eat on the go or to round off dinner.
